analysis.one_liner: Caps US greenhouse gas emissions using a tradeable permit system covering power plants, factories, and transportation fuel.
analysis.headline: The bill had 10 Senate sponsors including 2 Republicans and reached the Senate floor for debate in October 2003, but it was sent back to committee without a vote and never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The Climate Stewardship Act would have required electric utilities, factories, and petroleum refiners to hold one tradeable allowance for every metric ton of greenhouse gases they emit, starting in 2010 at roughly year-2000 emission levels and tightening toward 1990 levels after 2015. It also created a national public database of greenhouse gas emissions and funded climate research. A new nonprofit corporation would have sold government-issued allowances and used the proceeds for consumer rebates and transition help for workers who lost jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households gain two ways: the cap reduces the greenhouse gas pollution driving climate change, and the Climate Change Credit Corporation must use its allowance-trading proceeds to lower consumer energy costs through rebates and discounts, with preferential treatment for those who can least afford increases, plus transition assistance for dislocated workers. Companies that cut emissions or produce low-carbon energy profit from selling allowances they no longer need.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, via rebates and cleaner energy

how_it_helps.text: Caps emissions from the electric, industrial, commercial, and transportation-fuel sectors: from 2010 covered entities must submit one allowance per metric ton of greenhouse gases, with a total of 5,896 million metric tons for 2010-2015 and 5,123 million metric tons (roughly 1990 levels) thereafter.

Uses trading proceeds for consumers: the Climate Change Credit Corporation must use its allowances and trading proceeds to reduce costs borne by consumers, through buy-downs, rebates, and discounts, distributed across all regions and with preferential treatment for those least able to afford higher costs.

Provides transition assistance for dislocated workers and communities: at least 20 percent of trading proceeds in 2010 goes to job training, adjustment assistance, and community grants, declining gradually thereafter.
Requires covered entities to report their emissions to a national public greenhouse gas database, making polluters' emissions visible to the public for the first time.

Flexibility keeps costs down: firms can trade allowances across sectors, bank them, borrow against future reductions, and use limited foreign allowances, offsets, and sequestration credits for up to 15 percent of their obligation.

analysis.who_pays: Covered entities — electric generators, industrial and commercial facilities emitting over 10,000 metric tons per year, makers and importers of certain industrial gases, and petroleum refiners and importers — must hold allowances for their emissions or pay a civil penalty of three times the market value of missing allowances. Some of that compliance cost would pass through to consumers as higher energy prices, and the bill directs the allocation formula to weigh exactly that pass-through.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal utilities, refiners, and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: Energy compliance costs largely pass through to customers: the bill explicitly instructs allocation decisions to consider covered entities' ability to pass costs to their customers, meaning households and businesses would face some higher energy prices.

Nearly all allowances are given free to existing emitters rather than auctioned, so polluting companies receive valuable tradeable assets at no cost instead of the government raising revenue it could return to the public.

The cap is modest and porous: the 2010 level merely returns to roughly year-2000 emissions, and covered entities can satisfy up to 15 percent of their obligation with foreign allowances, offsets, and sequestration credits.
Coal-dependent regions and workers bear concentrated costs: the bill's own transition-assistance program exists because coal-heavy utilities and their communities were expected to be hit hardest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes a real but measured first step on climate: it caps major-source emissions, hands the public a transparent emissions database, and explicitly routes trading proceeds back to consumers and displaced workers rather than to the treasury or industry. Its weaknesses are that the initial cap is lenient, most allowances are gifted to the very companies being capped (which can create windfall asset value), and up to 15 percent of compliance can happen through foreign and offset credits that are hard to verify. On balance it protects consumers and workers more deliberately than most later cap-and-trade designs, but its environmental ambition was modest.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate pulled the bill out of committee, debated it for two days in late October 2003, then without a single senator objecting sent it right back to committee, where it sat until the Congress ended — it never came to an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: Senator Joseph Lieberman introduced the Climate Stewardship Act on January 9, 2003 with eight original cosponsors, including Republicans John McCain and Olympia Snowe, and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

On October 29, 2003 the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee was discharged from the bill by unanimous consent and the measure was laid before the full Senate — an unusually direct route to the floor for a bill the committee had never acted on.
The Senate considered the bill on October 29 and 30, 2003, then on October 30 rereferred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee by unanimous consent.
The bill received no further action and died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities, coal producers, and oil refiners came out ahead: the first-ever federal cap on their greenhouse gas emissions never took effect, so they avoided compliance costs and kept emitting without a price. Supporters of climate action got a floor debate and nothing more.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities and coal producers who avoided the cap

for.name: Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through two days of Senate floor debate in October 2003.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan leadership, and supported bringing it to the floor.

for.role: 7 Senate Democrats and Senator Olympia Snowe (R-ME)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 10 senators.

against.name: 55 of 100 Senators
against.role: Senators who voted against ending debate (cloture) on October 30, 2003
against.what_they_did: Voted 55-43 against the procedural vote needed to advance the bill to a final vote; cloture required 60, so the bill was sent back to committee.

against.name: Fossil fuel and electric utility industries
against.role: Coal, oil refining, and utility interests
against.what_they_did: Fought the first mandatory federal cap on their greenhouse gas emissions, the outcome the bill would have imposed on them.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory greenhouse gas emission limits throughout this period, setting the position of the administration whose allies controlled the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 10 sponsors included 2 Republicans and 7 Democrats, but when the Senate moved to advance it in October 2003, the vote failed 43-55, with opposition concentrated among Republicans joined by a minority of Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have capped their carbon dioxide emissions starting in 2010, their core cost concern, but allowed them allowances at no cost to existing facilities and flexibility to trade, bank, and borrow. The public's interest in lower emissions runs against the industry's interest in an unlimited permit to emit.

They would have had to submit allowances for every ton of greenhouse gas from the transportation fuel they sell, but the bill allocates the transportation-sector allowances to refiners and importers themselves at no cost, cushioning the hit. Consumers would bear part of the pass-through cost at the pump.
A cap that penalizes carbon dioxide from fossil fuels hits coal hardest, since it is the most carbon-intensive fuel for power generation; demand for coal-fired generation would decline.

The bill creates a market in tradeable allowances with a government-backed registry and serial-numbered credits, generating new business for brokers, verifiers, and exchanges. This market exists to achieve the public's emission-reduction goal.
By putting a price on each ton of greenhouse gases, the bill makes low- and zero-emission energy and efficiency investments more valuable relative to fossil generation.

Registered sequestration increases can satisfy part of utilities' compliance obligations, creating a new revenue stream for forest preservation, reforestation, and geological storage, subject to strict accounting rules.
